tagline: A point-of-care electrochemical sensor that quantifies individual protease activities in chronic wound exudate in about ten minutes.
summary: ProteaSign is a disposable-cartridge electrochemical diagnostic that separately measures MMP-9 (which degrades the extracellular matrix) and human neutrophil elastase (which degrades the growth factors needed for repair) in chronic wound fluid, turning wound assessment from a visual judgement into a measurement. The sensing interface is a gold electrode carrying methylene-blue-labelled, protease-cleavable peptides whose cleavage is read by square-wave voltammetry, with an independently anchored ferrocene reporter providing internal ratiometric normalisation and a matched non-cleavable peptide control on a second working electrode. The peptide sequences were not guessed: the team built a seven-protease machine-learning substrate predictor trained on 10,472 curated cleavage windows, and validated the predictions with two reprogrammable recombinant sfGFP protease biosensors. It won on the rare combination of genuinely publication-grade dry lab (cluster-aware cross-validation, Laplace-transform kinetics derivations, a physics-based SWV forward model), working hardware, and a human practices programme with over twenty named clinical and industrial stakeholders that visibly moved the design.
awards: Best Village Project nominee (Infectious Diseases / Therapeutics / Diagnostics / Oncology)

dry.frameworks: Three distinct modelling efforts, all unusually deep for high school. (1) A protease substrate predictor: for each of seven proteases (MMP-2, MMP-8, MMP-9, MMP-14, neutrophil elastase, LasB, and a pooled digestive serine protease group) they trained two additive scorers on 8-residue cleavage windows — an L2-regularised logistic regression on VHSE physicochemical descriptors (8 descriptors per residue, so 64 standardised features) and a BLOSUM62-smoothed position-specific scoring matrix — using 10,472 confirmed windows from MEROPS, Eckhard et al. 2016 proteomic MMP profiling, and a re-extracted LasB elastin-digestion table from Yang et al. 2015. Negatives were constructed 3:1 (half other proteases' real windows, half random Swiss-Prot 8-mers at natural amino-acid frequencies). (2) A surface-bound enzyme kinetics model: they derived both the steady-state solution and the exact biexponential solution for Michaelis-Menten kinetics on a surface-attached substrate using Laplace transforms and partial-fraction decomposition, then proved analytically and numerically that the steady-state approximation is only valid as their single parameter lambda approaches 1. (3) A square-wave voltammetry forward model (swv_forward_model.py) that computes net SWV current from probe-level physics — about 3.1e10 probes at 7.4 nm spacing, with a 1.4 nm methylene-blue lateral excursion used to justify treating probes as non-interacting.
dry.dataviz: The substrate predictor page ends in a live in-browser scorer ('Try It — Score a Peptide'): you type a peptide, mark the scissile bond, and every protease in the panel scores it as you type, with warm/cool per-position attribution bars that sum exactly to the logit and the PSSM score, and grey bars for unknown (gapped) positions. The sensor probe itself is shown scored at every bond by the MMP-9 and elastase models, with the P4-to-P4' window shaded and the actual cut marked. The SWV page carries an interactive forward-model plot where moving across reads every predicted current curve at one potential. Results are presented as out-of-fold ROC curves, precision-recall curves against a 0.25 prior, and held-out percentile distributions against a uniform null, plus paired difference plots with 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals where a filled marker means the interval excludes zero. Equations are rendered in KaTeX and the human practices page uses globe.gl.
dry.datascience: The evaluation methodology is the real achievement and is more careful than most undergraduate iGEM dry lab. They recognised that near-duplicate cleavage windows cause data leakage under ordinary K-fold CV, so they defined Hamming-distance clusters (any pair with d_H <= 2, taken as connected components, found in near-linear time via a 3+3+2-block pigeonhole trick with union-find) and used stratified group 5-fold splitting whole clusters, with a nested 3-fold inner CV to pick the regularisation strength C per protease, and the null percentile distribution and PSSM rebuilt per outer fold to avoid leaking into the background. They separated two questions — Detection (held-out positives vs random background) and Discrimination (held-out positives vs another protease's confirmed sites), noting the latter is what actually matters for a multiplexed sensor. They derived and Monte-Carlo-verified an analytic ceiling on measured AUROC under false negatives (measured AUROC <= 1 - pi/2 for a fraction pi of mislabelled negatives), ran three controls (label shuffle collapsing AUROC to 0.49-0.53; composition-only ablation showing e.g. 0.664 vs 0.874 for MMP-2 but 0.886 vs 0.877 for LasB because 76% of its positives come from elastin; and random vs cluster-aware folds, where LasB drops 0.886 to 0.879 once leakage is removed). Scores from the two models are converted to percentiles against 100,000 random Swiss-Prot background windows so they are comparable across proteases, combined by harmonic mean (high only when both are high), and reported as a 'specificity margin' = target consensus percentile minus the strongest competitor's. They also published an explicit list of eight assumptions and limitations, including that additivity costs at most 0.007 AUROC against gradient-boosted trees, that VHSE PCA captures only 64-79% of the full positional signal, and that the harmonic-mean consensus was reasoned rather than validated.
dry.software: The substrate predictor is released as a protease-agnostic Python package (modules spred.data, spred.model, spred.pssm, spred.train, spred.validation, spred.evaluation, spred.panel) that another team retrains on its own protease panel's known substrates on a basic laptop in a few hours; the team explicitly frames it as a reusable contribution. Hardware: a handheld reader built around the Analog Devices AD5940 electrochemical analogue front end with an nRF52840 microcontroller and a TI TMUX1104 4:1 precision multiplexer, sequentially interrogating four working electrodes against a shared reference and counter electrode, with full KiCad schematics (5 sheets) and an exported bill of materials released as PDF. The hardware builds on the open-source Biocoin wearable multiplexed biosensing platform (github.com/ProfDrewHall/Biocoin; Hack & Hall, npj Biosensing 2026). They also contribute two reprogrammable recombinant protease biosensors with swappable substrate 'cassettes': pES-01 (FLAG-sfGFP / peptide / C-terminal His6, read by Ni-NTA depletion, ELISA, Western blot or SDS-PAGE) and pDUAL (split-sfGFP with GFP11 embedded in an eglin c surface loop, giving a fluorescence readout). Code and wiki at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/eton-college-uk.

good.publicEngagement: A genuinely reusable education portfolio rather than a set of one-off visits. 'What If?' is a team-written and illustrated comic modelled on Marvel's What If...? series, built directly from the four ideas children drew at the Eton Porny workshop (colour-changing plants, bacteria making medicines, programmable cells, healing wounds); over 350 printed copies were distributed in two months and it was translated into two further languages. A 58-page Activities Handbook of printable exercises at graded difficulty, with instructions and answer keys written in conversation with a secondary school teacher, was inspired by Leiden iGEM 2025's approach to reusable materials. 'Bio-Detectives' is a museum-sabotage mystery workshop for Year 8 in which teams work five stations — reconstructing DNA sequences, exploring protein production, critiquing flawed experiments, comparing lab labels, and modelling genetic control through AND/OR/NOR gates — and must explain their reasoning to unlock each piece of evidence, ending in a fixed-budget redesign task; student and facilitator packs plus the presentation are released so it can be rerun. Year 11 volunteers facilitated and reported their own gains ('I'm not a science student but still really enjoyed it because of the mystery format'). They report honestly that the content was too hard for pupils who had not yet met DNA and recommend targeting Year 10/11 instead. Other sessions: a hands-on goat-DNA genetic modification build for 34 Year 5 pupils at St George's Windsor (physically assembling glowing / curly-hair / spider-silk gene templates from spare nucleotides), an edible animal-cell modelling workshop with a published allergen risk assessment, protease kits for a carers' workshop, street interviews (8 of N respondents had no personal experience of chronic wounds), and biosafety videos.
good.ihp: Over twenty named stakeholders across wound care, electrochemistry, health economics, regulation and patient advocacy, with a 'pinpoint / event / action' structure that states what changed. Concrete examples: Dr Anatoliy Markiv (King's College London) moved them off pET-24a(+) to pSB1C3 as a reusable starting plasmid, reviewed their primers and proposed a better substrate-swapping method, and pointed them to the split-GFP protease-sensing paper that became their second design cycle; he also required construct sequences for biosafety assessment before permitting experiments. Dr Ben Bullen (podiatry) cemented the reusable-reader / disposable-cartridge split and the ~20 microlitre sample volume, and set a 15-minute workflow target against the team's estimated 30 minutes — which the team records as an unmet goal requiring shorter incubation. Ms Kathleen Leak (tissue viability) and Trish Idensohn drove the requirement for fast readouts and simple operating procedures, which produced the cartridge's standardised metering, dilution and incubation steps before SWV acquisition. Dr Honda Hsu (plastic surgeon, Taiwan) confirmed the device fits a real clinical workflow and his account of delegated wound care created an explicit usability requirement that routine dressing-change staff, not just specialists, must be able to run it. Dr Kevin Lye (Accorto Regulatory Solutions) and Dr Douglas Queen (health economics of wound care) covered the regulatory and reimbursement path; Dr Martin Peacock (Zimmer and Peacock) and Professor Kevin Lam (synthetic electrochemistry, Greenwich) and Dr Ana Maria Totea advised on electrodes and liquid handling; Professor Keith Harding (Cardiff), Professor Steven Jeffery (Pioneer Wound Clinics), Professor Dato Harikrishna Nair, Professor Paul Davis (co-founder of Mologic) and Professor Eleanor Stride (Oxford biomedical engineering) reviewed the clinical and device case. Patient and charity voices included 'Bob', a person living with a chronic wound, Breakthrough T1D and Diabetes Scotland. Feedback also reinforced measuring cleavage rate with calibration across known enzyme concentrations. The anonymised 'David' narrative on the description page is explicitly constructed from real accounts heard through these conversations.
good.realWorld: The implementation page is a structured device risk assessment rather than a business pitch: it enumerates infection transfer through reusable components, pain or damage to fragile healing tissue, allergic reaction to wound-contacting materials, unnecessary anxiety or treatment escalation from false positives, and exposure of identifiable patient data, each with a named mitigation (prefer single-use patient-contacting components, biocompatibility assessment of all wound-contacting materials, clinically justified interpretation criteria with evaluated specificity and false-positive rates, calibration and quality-control procedures with error alerts and clear invalid-test instructions, minimised personal data collection with access restriction and retention policies). The intended route to market is a reusable reader plus disposable cartridge for community wound care — GPs, wound-care nurses, podiatrists and carers — positioned to guide selection of the existing protease-modulating dressings (e.g. UrgoStart) and to track proteolytic activity over time alongside wound size. Costing came from the KiCad bill of materials plus estimated enclosure and reagent costs. The team is candid that clinical validation, bacterial confounding of the chosen peptides, and testing on real clinical samples all remain outstanding. A Smith + Nephew work experience business insight day and an Imperial iGEM mini-jamboree (24 August, UK and European teams) fed the commercial framing.

gemsTakeaway: Copy their evaluation discipline, not just their model: before reporting any ML metric, cluster near-duplicate sequences by Hamming distance and split whole clusters across folds, then run a label-shuffle control and an ablation that strips the information you claim to be using — three cheap steps that turn a high-school classifier from a number into evidence. Their second transferable move is shipping the model as a live in-browser scorer with per-position attribution bars, so a judge or clinician can interrogate the prediction instead of taking the AUROC on trust.
